cohorts.comparison: HUDA, Burnstein and FernCare offer relatively legible uninsured clinical access; Community First adds outer-metro access, Hope Clinic adds documented Westland care, and ACCESS adds differentiated language/community reach despite a broad portfolio. CHASS, Covenant, Advantage, MyCare and Honor are close integrated-care alternatives, with larger public/payer scope to resolve. SAY, World Medical Relief, Leader Dogs, Bear Lake and St. Patrick retain distinct mechanisms but substantial wider-scope, mobility/recreation or donated-resource attribution questions. Selection is research tractability and potential, not measured superior efficacy.

Corktown and Ruth Ellis are prioritized for differentiated local health and vulnerable-population access. Vivent’s current Metro Detroit delivery is a strong reserve, but the national merged payee and pharmacy/public HIV financing complicate a local ordinary-gift model. Clinical partner overlap, PrEP retention, viral suppression and housing links must not be added as independent full effects.

Detroit Recovery Project, Harm Reduction Michigan and Face Addiction Now prioritize concrete local overdose/recovery pathways. CARE and Mariners Inn are close treatment/peer alternatives; SHAR and Rescue Mission remain relevant full-service comparators. Actual added high-risk delivery, alternative rescue, treatment retention, public naloxone and finite post-rescue survival determine value—not one kit, contact or rescue equals a life.

Common Ground and Starfish prioritize crisis access and delivered child/family clinical pathways. Hegira, Judson, Children’s Center, Oakland Family Services, Guidance Center, MiSide and Macomb Family Services are strong clinical reserves with public/payer and broad-portfolio constraints. Affirmations offers differentiated LGBTQ therapy, Gilda’s cancer support, Gesher residential/community support, and Rose Hill Foundation a clinical-provider funding route requiring full leveraged costs. Counseling sessions, social support and residential days are not interchangeable health units.

BMBFA and Birth Detroit prioritize concrete perinatal support and clinical delivery. PPMI is a strong direct-clinical reserve whose current funding/legal changes require early attention; Mothering Justice and MOASH provide longer policy/training pathways, while Detroit Parent Network supports family capacity. Do not assume midwife attendance or breastfeeding contact produces a fixed mortality gain; substitution, clinical safety and finite maternal/infant effects matter.

HOPE’s recuperative shelter creates a particularly testable health pathway. Wayne Metro, Cass, COTS, Phoenix, Covenant House, Lighthouse, NSO, SOCH, Community Housing Network, Noah, Samaritas, OLHSA, MCREST, Livingston Catholic and Blue Water are substantive differentiated alternatives. Their wider bundles, public contracts, rental/capital transfers and overlapping clinical partners make shelter or rent counts insufficient for ranking. No outer-county or youth population is judged less deserving.

Turning Point, HAVEN and LACASA prioritize geographically differentiated survivor services with plausible clinical/safety pathways. First Step, Blue Water Safe Horizons, LACADA, Alternatives for Girls and MCEDSV remain close alternatives, including coalition and specialized youth work. Public victim-service funding, counterfactual shelter/legal access, repeat users and adverse safety responses require explicit modeling.

DJC, UCHC and Lakeshore prioritize direct legal/housing links while retaining systemic leverage. Michigan Legal Services, Legal Aid and Defender, MAP and Disability Rights Michigan are strong alternative legal pathways; Freedom House adds humanitarian stabilization, Sugar Law worker protections and MLPP policy. Consolidate affiliated programs, include public right-to-counsel and implementation response, and never translate recovered dollars one-for-one into QALYs.

We the People of Detroit and Detroit Greenways prioritize locally traceable water access and injury/exposure pathways. DWEJ, Freshwater Future, MEC, Ecology Center, Clean Water Fund, EMEAC and Friends of the Rouge retain policy/exposure and ecological alternatives with larger coalition, geographic or biological-translation burdens. Public capital and regulation would continue in the counterfactual; all climate/national/watershed benefits are not local.

Gleaners’ healthcare/nutrition initiatives merit the first clinical-food comparison; Forgotten Harvest is the close food-rescue alternative. Baldwin, Focus HOPE, Capuchin, DBCFSN, Keep Growing Detroit, Brilliant Cities, Matrix and Fish and Loaves offer distinct access/community pathways. Banking, rescue, pantry and consumption are linked stages, not each entitled to all health. Broad social portfolios and public food replacement remain in scope.
